content: Two experimental HIV vaccine regimens were evaluated. The first combined DNA with protein-based candidate vaccines, while the second combined DNA, modified vaccinia virus Ankara, and protein-based candidate vaccines. Additional details on the pipeline of HIV vaccine and prevention candidates can be found in Annexes 1 and 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) has outlined preferred product characteristics for monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) for HIV prevention. These characteristics address the public health need for mAbs in the context of existing interventions. Current interventions proven effective in reducing HIV infection risk include consistent and correct use of male and female condoms, voluntary medical male circumcision, clean needles and syringes for people who inject drugs, medications for opioid use disorder, treatment of people with HIV to prevent onward transmission (treatment as prevention), and the use of antiretroviral (ARV) medicines as oral pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP). In 2012, WHO issued guidance for the use of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate and emtricitabine (TDF/FTC) as oral PrEP for serodiscordant couples, men, and transgender women who have sex with men and are at high risk of HIV. By 2015, this guidance was expanded to include all individuals at substantial risk of HIV infection, defined as a population group with an incidence greater than 3 per 100 person-years. As of March 2021, approximately 1,115,000 individuals had initiated oral PrEP, falling short of the WHO/UNAIDS target of initiating at least 3,000,000 people by 2020. Among 69 countries implementing PrEP, 81% reported at least one barrier to PrEP access. The efficacy of oral PrEP with TDF/FTC has varied widely across clinical trials and populations. Challenges with adherence to daily or event-driven regimens, side effects, and stigma associated with using the same product for both treatment and prevention have contributed to non-adherence or discontinuation, significantly impacting PrEP's effectiveness. In October 2019, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved emtricitabine/tenofovir alafenamide (F/TAF) for daily oral PrEP to reduce the risk of HIV infection through sex, excluding those engaging in receptive vaginal sex. Despite strong adherence in clinical trials, F/TAF may face real-world implementation challenges similar to TDF/FTC due to comparable product profiles and daily dosing requirements. Efficacy data on F/TAF as a PrEP agent for women or people who inject drugs (PWID) are lacking. Two Phase 3 trials examined the efficacy of the dapivirine vaginal ring (DPV-VR) as a monthly prevention option, showing a 30-46% reduction in HIV infection risk among African women. However, no protection was observed among women aged 18–21, likely due to lower adherence levels in women under 25. An open-label extension study (DREAM) demonstrated increased product use compared to the previous Phase 3 RING study, with modeling data suggesting a 63% reduction in women's HIV-1 risk. The DPV-VR received a positive scientific opinion from the European Medicines Agency (EMA) and WHO prequalification in November 2020 for use in women at higher HIV risk aged 18 years and older. WHO recommended the DPV-VR as an additional prevention choice for women at substantial HIV risk as part of combination prevention approaches. Results from the HIV Prevention Trials Network (HPTN) 083 Phase 3 study showed that long-acting cabotegravir (CAB-LA), administered every two months, was 66% more effective in preventing HIV acquisition than daily oral PrEP with TDF/FTC among men who have sex with men (MSM) and transgender women. CAB-LA was authorized as a monthly treatment in combination with rilpivirine by the European Commission in December 2020 and by the FDA in January 2021. Rolling regulatory submission with the FDA for CAB-LA's prevention indication began in May 2021. Acceptability research suggests that delivering PrEP through a long-acting injectable product could address challenges associated with daily oral regimens. Women, particularly young women in sub-Saharan Africa, report a preference for injectable prevention technologies over monthly vaginal rings or daily pills. However, some studies of CAB-LA have cited concerns regarding the frequency of clinic visits and user preferences for fewer injections. Additionally, the injectable contraception literature documents high rates of non-adherence among women using analogous injectable hormonal contraceptives, suggesting that a long-acting injectable PrEP formulation would not completely solve adherence challenges in regions where HIV is endemic. Implementation challenges also include the requirement for a daily oral lead-in period of four weeks before CAB-LA administration. For those discontinuing use, there are concerns about the product's potentially prolonged declining serum concentrations, which have been demonstrated to last more than a year in some individuals. This could increase the risk of drug resistance and selection of escape mutants that endanger the drug class for treatment indications if individuals contract HIV. Alongside CAB-LA, additional promising long-acting ARVs are in the pipeline. In early 2021, Merck launched the IMPOWER 22 Phase 3 study in sub-Saharan Africa and the USA to evaluate the efficacy and safety of islatravir, a nucleoside reverse transcriptase translocation inhibitor, administered orally once monthly as PrEP in cisgender women at high risk for HIV-1 infection. The IMPOWER 24 study will evaluate other key populations, including MSM and transgender women. However, in December 2021, the FDA put all studies for islatravir on hold due to unexpected decreases in total lymphocyte and CD4+ T-cell counts in some study participants. Gilead is planning to evaluate the use of lenacapavir, a long-acting HIV-1 capsid inhibitor, as an injectable PrEP option administered every six months in cisgender adolescent girls and young women. In a separate trial, lenacapavir will also be studied in cisgender men, transgender individuals, and gender nonbinary persons who have sex with men. The use of monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) to treat and prevent disease is one of the most rapidly growing areas of biomedical research. More than 100 mAbs for different indications have been licensed or submitted for regulatory review in the USA and European Union alone, and mAbs are now the single-largest class of molecules undergoing clinical investigation. In 2018, ibalizumab (TNX-355) became the first mAb to receive FDA approval as salvage therapy in HIV-positive patients whose viruses are resistant to multiple existing ARV drugs. In 2019, it was also approved by the EMA for use in combination with other ARVs for the treatment of adults infected with multidrug-resistant HIV-1 infection for whom it is otherwise not possible to construct a suppressive antiviral regimen. Broadly neutralizing antibodies (bNAbs) derive from naturally occurring antibodies with potent neutralizing activity against a broad array of HIV strains in vitro. Research suggests structural modifications to mAbs can increase their breadth, potency, and half-life, potentially extending their duration of protection and enabling dosing on a bimonthly, quarterly, or semi-annual basis. Given their favorable safety and pharmacokinetic profiles, mAbs offer potential advantages over the use of ARVs for the prevention of HIV. Since mAbs have a different mechanism of protection than ARV drugs, they could mitigate the risk of resistance to ARVs and minimize stigma associated with the use of ARV-based products for prevention. It is also possible that mAbs might have fewer adverse effects than certain ARV drugs, particularly during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Preclinical studies suggest that even relatively low concentrations of potent anti-HIV-1 neutralizing antibodies can block infection. Several mAbs with significant breadth and potency that target different HIV envelope epitopes have entered clinical trials and are being evaluated for their potential as long-acting alternatives to ARVs for HIV prevention and therapy. The first bNAb to be tested for efficacy in HIV prevention was VRC01. Phase 1 studies of VRC01 administered as a monthly or bimonthly intravenous (IV) infusion or as a biweekly subcutaneous injection found it to be safe, well-tolerated, and capable of maintaining serum concentrations consistent with neutralization of the majority of tested HIV strains. VRC01 has also demonstrated promising safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics in HIV-exposed infants. Based on these promising results, the NIAID HIV Vaccine Trials Network (HVTN) and HPTN-sponsored AMP efficacy trials evaluated whether providing VRC01 as an IV infusion every eight weeks is safe, tolerable, and effective at preventing HIV infection. However, the primary endpoint of prevention of HIV infection did not achieve a significant difference between the intervention and the control in the trial. Investigators found that only 30% of the HIV strains circulating in the regions where the trials were conducted were sensitive to VRC01. Additional findings were that in the AMP trial, virus sensitivity to VRC01 neutralization appeared to correlate with protective efficacy. The trials also offered insight into the concentration of antibodies required to afford protection against HIV in humans. Antibodies and engineered antibody-like molecules that are more potent, broader, or longer-lasting than VRC01 are currently in early clinical testing. Given that neutralization escape from single antibodies occurs readily, combinations of bNAbs targeting different epitopes may be necessary to achieve broad and durable protection against HIV.
